To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we have shown how to predict molecular packing and charge transport in organic semiconducting crystals by means of first-principles quantum chemistry; (2) we have shown that the packing motifs of functionalized molecules can be predicted with a good accuracy; (3) we have shown the importance of the functional groups on the charge transport properties of organic crystals; (4) we have demonstrated the possibility to predict the packing motifs of other functionalized molecules.

(i) dispersion-corrected DFT methods can be used to determine the molecular packing of tetracene derivatives; (ii) the molecular packing of these derivatives can be predicted on the basis of a small set of functionalized tetracenes; (iii) the charge mobilities of these derivatives can differ by orders of magnitude.

the packing of organic semiconducting materials can be predicted from the first-principles and that the charge transport properties of these materials can be accurately predicted from the same theoretical approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new methodology that can be used to study organic semiconducting materials, which are of paramount interest for the development of electronic devices.
the development of computational tools that can be used to predict charge-transport properties of organic semiconducting materials.

the development of computational protocols to predict molecular packing and charge transport properties of organic materials, which are essential to understand the behavior of organic-based electronic materials and devices.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the packing of the organic molecules in the crystal is a key factor to determine the charge mobility in organic semiconducting materials.
the packing of the tetracenes in the crystalline state is not only influenced by the nature of the functional group, but also by the molecular conformation.
this study demonstrates that the packing of organic semiconducting molecules can be predicted by first principles and that the resulting charge mobility is a function of the chemical substitution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combination of DFT calculations with the inclusion of dispersion effects allows for an accurate prediction of the molecular packing and the charge transport parameters of organic semiconducting materials.
we are able to predict the molecular packing of organic semiconducting materials, as well as the charge mobilities of such materials, from first principles.

the combination of dispersion-corrected density functional theory calculations and the analysis of the charge transport parameters allows for the prediction of the packing motifs of functionalized tetracene derivatives and the estimation of the hole mobility of these materials.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a reliable description of charge transport in organic semiconducting materials can be achieved by a quantum-chemical approach, which is able to describe the interplay between electronic properties and crystal structure.
the charge mobility in the organic semiconducting material is not only dependent on the molecular packing but is strongly related to the molecular structure as well.
the molecular structure, and not just the molecular packing, has a significant impact on the charge transport properties.
